name: Hindulotine from Hindulotine
description: Hindulotine from Hindu Control joins the hands after the arm loops over the raised foot. The bottom guard player closes a leg-in guillotine and releases on a tap.
summary: The Hindulotine is Ben Eddy's leg-in guillotine from Hindu Control, using an arm loop over the raised rubber-guard foot and around the shoulder to close a neck enclosure.
target_area: Neck, enclosed by the arm and raised rubber-guard leg
overview:
The bottom guard player keeps a raised knee near the torso and loops an elbow over the foot, bringing the hand around the opponent's shoulder. Hindu Control is the setup; Hindulotine is the choke. Ben Eddy's early reverse-gable demonstration and later S-grip explanation are teaching variants, not a license to force any hand grip through a closed gap.

Turn onto the hip and keep the knee close so the foot is reached through body position. Bring the elbow above the raised foot and the hand around the shoulder into the head-control space. Retain the leg-and-arm enclosure without adding neck pressure while locating the second hand. Use the demonstrated S-grip or the earlier reverse-gable variation without wrenching the wrist or knee.

Drill the arm path with no choke pressure first. Protect the high knee, avoid cervical twisting, and release both the grip and raised leg immediately on any stop signal.

Instructional sources: [Ben Eddy — Hindu Control to Hindulotine](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y5ZQNgG2hNc); [Ben Eddy — later Hindulotine S-grip clarification](https://www.10thplanetjj.com/forum/printthread.php?page=2&pp=10&t=22650).

This neck enclosure can load the sides of the neck as a vascular choke, and misplaced forearm pressure can also compress the windpipe. Neither pressure type is a training target: rehearse the grip without squeezing, and release before the partner needs to tolerate throat or neck pressure.

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: what hip orientation helps bring the raised foot within reach?
flashcards.answer: Rolled onto one side rather than flat on the back. Use the hip angle to bring the supported leg within reach. Keep the knee close and avoid hauling the foot against a fixed knee.
flashcards.answer_line: Rolled onto one side rather than flat on the back

plausible: Square and flat while pulling the ankle toward the face
Turned away while the high knee stays pinned
trap: Lifted into a neck stack to shorten the reach

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: after your elbow passes the raised foot, where does that hand travel?
flashcards.answer: Around the opponent's shoulder toward the head. Route the hand around the shoulder into the head-control space after the elbow clears the foot. Keep the knee supported rather than pulling the foot against a fixed knee.
flashcards.answer_line: Around the opponent's shoulder toward the head

plausible: Under your own thigh toward the near hip
Down the opponent's back toward the waist
trap: Across their wrist while leaving the shoulder outside

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: where must the controlling elbow pass relative to your raised foot?
flashcards.answer: Above the supported foot. The controlling elbow passes over the raised foot, then the hand travels around the shoulder. Preserve an unloaded leg-and-arm connection while finding the second hand.

plausible: Below the arch while the knee stays wide
Outside the shin toward the hip
trap: Behind your own thigh with the hand above the head

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: which two connections appear in Ben Eddy's early and later teaching?
flashcards.answer: Reverse-gable in the early lesson; S-grip later. Use the demonstrated S-grip or the earlier reverse-gable variation without wrenching the wrist or knee.
flashcards.answer_line: Reverse-gable in the early lesson; S-grip later

plausible: S-grip early; rear-naked-choke figure-four later
Collar grip early; reverse-gable only in no-gi
trap: A single unchanged palm-to-wrist grip in both

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: how should connected elbow movement remove the last slack?
flashcards.answer: Lift to close space while keeping the neck aligned. Lift the connected elbows only enough to close space; stop immediately if the pressure becomes a neck twist.
flashcards.answer_line: Lift to close space while keeping the neck aligned

plausible: Raise sharply until the head bends backward
Twist both hands while holding the high knee fixed
trap: Pull the head sideways against the leg

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: what must release on a tap even if the opponent passed your lower leg?
flashcards.answer: Both hands and the raised-leg enclosure. Release the whole enclosure at the first tap or change in responsiveness, including if the opponent has passed the lower leg.
flashcards.answer_line: Both hands and the raised-leg enclosure

plausible: Only the lower foot that was passed
Only the support fingers while the first arm keeps pulling
trap: Only the hip connection while the head remains caught

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: why can hauling the foot from flat hips load your own knee?
flashcards.answer: A fixed knee takes motion that should come from the hip. Turn onto the hip and support the close knee rather than pulling a distant foot across the joint. Eddy's entry keeps the raised knee supported as the hip supplies the angle.
flashcards.answer_line: A fixed knee takes motion that should come from the hip

plausible: Flat hips automatically give the knee more rotation
A stronger ankle pull always frees the hip first
trap: The raised foot can be forced farther whenever the neck stays loose

flashcards.question: Hindulotine attack: what distinguishes Hindu Control from the named submission attempt?
flashcards.answer: Loading the connected enclosure changes hold to choke. Hindu Control is the setup; Hindulotine is the choke. Ben Eddy's early reverse-gable demonstration and later S-grip explanation are teaching variants, not a license to force any hand grip through a closed gap.
flashcards.answer_line: Loading the connected enclosure changes hold to choke

plausible: The hold already guarantees a finish without a hand connection
Adding a jacket grip supplies the required shoulder-to-neck compression
trap: The submission requires both legs to leave the opponent entirely

flashcards.question: Hindulotine practice: how far should the raised knee move from your ribs when reaching the foot?
flashcards.answer: Close to the torso with support. Maintain the knee hug/support and use hip rotation to shorten the distance. The first repetitions should also include a complete release without choke pressure.
flashcards.answer_line: Close to the torso with support

plausible: Flared away while the hand pulls the foot inward
Fixed on the floor while the ankle moves across the face
trap: Straightened away from the hips to increase reach

flashcards.question: Hindulotine practice: which connection may remain around the neck after your lower leg is passed?
flashcards.answer: The high leg joined to the controlling arm. Passing the lower leg does not necessarily open the high leg-and-arm connection. Release the whole enclosure on a tap even if the opponent has gained lower-body position.
flashcards.answer_line: The high leg joined to the controlling arm

plausible: Only the lower-leg hook around the hips
A low ankle crossing around the waist
trap: The knee shield across the chest with the high leg released

defender.name: from Hindulotine Defender
defender.description: Hindulotine from Hindulotine (defender): An elbow passing over the raised foot toward your shoulder signals the leg-in guillotine setup. Use an early inside frame before both hands close around the neck enclosure.
defender.overview:
The bottom guard player keeps a raised knee near the torso and loops an elbow over the foot, bringing the hand around the opponent's shoulder. Hindu Control is the setup; Hindulotine is the choke. Ben Eddy's early reverse-gable demonstration and later S-grip explanation are teaching variants, not a license to force any hand grip through a closed gap.

An elbow passing over the raised foot toward your shoulder signals the leg-in guillotine setup. Use an early inside frame before both hands close around the neck enclosure. Avoid turning the head sharply against the fixed leg and forearm.

Address the head-and-leg connection instead of assuming a lower-body guard pass solves the choke. Stop before neck pain, dizziness, or reduced awareness; positional progress does not cancel the choke. Rebuild posture and guard-passing frames only after the head has been freed.

Drill the arm path with no choke pressure first. Protect the high knee, avoid cervical twisting, and release both the grip and raised leg immediately on any stop signal.

The early escape denies the finishing hand connection and clears the head-and-leg enclosure. Passing the lower leg does not free the neck; tap if the upper enclosure is already closed.

Protect the neck while denying the finishing hand: keep the head aligned and an inside arm between your neck and the closing enclosure. A chin position alone cannot undo the raised-leg and arm connection.

flashcards.question: Hindulotine defense: which approach of the opponent's arm signals the leg-in guillotine?
flashcards.answer: Elbow over their raised foot toward your shoulder. An elbow passing over the raised foot toward your shoulder signals the leg-in guillotine setup.
flashcards.answer_line: Elbow over their raised foot toward your shoulder

plausible: Elbow beneath your thigh toward the far knee
Hand behind your hip with their raised leg lowered
trap: Both forearms outside the head and below your ribs

flashcards.question: Hindulotine defense: what should an early inside frame obstruct?
flashcards.answer: The two hands joining around the neck enclosure. Use an early inside frame before both hands close around the neck enclosure.
flashcards.answer_line: The two hands joining around the neck enclosure

plausible: The attacker's lower heel returning to the mat
Your own elbow bending toward your ribs
trap: The opponent's free toes touching your hip

flashcards.question: Hindulotine defense: why should you avoid a sharp head turn against the secured grip?
flashcards.answer: The fixed leg and forearm restrain the neck during a turn. Avoid turning the head sharply against the fixed leg and forearm.
flashcards.answer_line: The fixed leg and forearm restrain the neck during a turn

plausible: A head turn always slides the raised foot away
The hand connection controls only your upper arm
trap: A raised knee prevents the grip compressing the neck

flashcards.question: Hindulotine defense: does clearing the lower leg alone establish that the choke has opened?
flashcards.answer: No; the upper enclosure can remain closed. The hands and raised leg may retain the head even after a lower-body pass. Continue to recognize that enclosure and tap if it is secured.
flashcards.answer_line: No; the upper enclosure can remain closed

plausible: Yes; passing the hips removes the neck connection
Yes; the raised foot must release when the low leg clears
trap: Yes; side position prevents the joined hands from loading

flashcards.question: Hindulotine defense: what must the partner do after your tap before you move away?
flashcards.answer: Open both hands and lower the raised leg. The whole enclosure must open before the bodies turn or separate. A positional pass is not itself evidence that the neck has been released.
flashcards.answer_line: Open both hands and lower the raised leg

plausible: Keep the high foot fixed while loosening only one finger
Hold the neck loop until you turn to face them
trap: Release the lower-leg hook while preserving the head connection
